column4: The section describes 94:1 as a question that recalls a completed favor for its addressee. 93:6 uses the same retrospective question stance for the same addressee, recalling that God found him an orphan and sheltered him; it places the chest opening among remembered personal favors.

The source section defines root ص د ر as the bodily chest and says the image first shows a body being opened. This ayah locates the hearts within the breasts and contrasts them with eyes that may see while hearts are blind; it links the bodily chest to inward reception while marking a distinct kind of blindness.

The source section traces ش ر ح through cutting and spreading, then says a gathered thing opens and its interior is revealed. In this ayah, after hardened hearts are compared to stone, some rocks split and water comes out; it gives a concrete nonlexical parallel of a hard, closed body opening to release what is within.

The source section's dictionary sense of ش ر ح includes spreading difficult speech so its hidden meaning appears. This ayah says each person will meet a record-book “مَنشُورًا”; an opened text makes its previously unseen contents available to its reader.

After the spread record in 17:13, this ayah tells the person “اقْرَأْ كِتَابَكَ.” Its own contribution is the reading of the exposed contents, completing the section's image of difficult words opened so their meaning can be seen.

The source section describes the opening of a folded thing and the exposing of what is inside, and gives difficult speech as a case of that operation. This ayah pictures the records spread open at judgment, a specific scene where written contents cease to be hidden.

The source section labels root و ز ر for 94:2's burden and explains its dictionary image as a bundle formed by spreading and filling a garment. This ayah says one who turns away from the reminder will carry a burden on the Day of Resurrection, a concrete use of that load-image.

Following the burden in 20:100, this ayah calls it an evil load on the Day of Resurrection. The source section's dictionary gloss treats 94:2's burden as a packed bundle; this continuation gives the weight-bearing result its own force.

The source section names root ص د ر and says opening speech can make hidden meanings visible. This ayah joins God establishing truth by His words with His knowledge of “ذَاتِ الصُّدُورِ,” connecting revealed truth with what is held inside breasts.

The source section defines root ص د ر as the bodily chest and notes a person who suffers chest trouble. This ayah says God heals the breasts of a believing people in the battle setting; it gives a direct bodily-chest counterpart to the section's opening of a constricted space.

The source section names root ص د ر for the chest and says it is opened to receive truth; it also describes explanation as making hidden meaning visible. This ayah calls revelation a healing for what is in the breasts, alongside admonition and guidance, joining revealed speech to the inner chest.

The source section describes the opened chest as a space whose interior is exposed and cleared. This ayah says rancor is removed from the residents' breasts before describing them as brothers facing one another; the cleared chest gives a specific counterpart to the section's opened interior.

The source section names root ص د ر and describes opening as creating room within. This ayah says rancor is removed from the people of Paradise's breasts as they acknowledge that God guided them; the emptied interior makes room for reconciled fellowship.
